newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil bankers welcome new Cenbank chief nominee.
newsitem.headline: Brazil bankers welcome new Cenbank chief nominee.

text.p: Brazil's financial community on Tuesday applauded Gustavo Franco's nomination as the new Central Bank chief saying it sent a clear signal the government was committed to the economic policy now in place.

Bankers said the 41 year-old Franco, currently a member of the Central Bank board and responsible for International Affairs, is a known quantity, widely respected for his intelect and outspoken views.
Franco's designation, which must still be confirmed by the Senate, was announced by Finance Minister Pedro Malan at a news conference on Tuesday evening.
He replaces Gustavo Loyola, a career Central Bank bureaucrat who over the lasst two years has overseen the dramatic shake-up of Brazil's financial industry.

"Gustavo Franco is a natural replacement. I think the President and the Finance Minister intended to send a very clear signal to the market -- and that was that there will be no change in economic policy," said Ricardo Gallo, vice president of BankBoston Brazil.

Analysts said Loyola's exit came as no surprise. Permanently under attack from enemies in Congress and exhausted by his efforts to restructure the country's overbanked economy, it was common knowledge in financial circles that Loyola had had enough.

Bankers were full of praise for the outgoing Central Bank head. "Loyola was one of the best Central Bank presidents we have ever had," said Luiz Chrysostomo de Olivera Filho, a partner at Banco Patrimonio.
"He steered a steady ship through a very difficult period. One Gustavo steps out, another steps in. Both are in perfect harmony," he said.
Confident and articulate, bankers said the new Central Bank head's style will be in sharp contrast to that of Loyola.
"Gustavo Franco is a strong personality who will not shy away from controversy. He has a clear idea of where he wants to take the economy and will defend his views aggressively," said Gallo.

While remembering that President Fernando Henrique Cardoso was sometimes forced to publicly rap Franco over the knuckles for speaking out of line, bankers said they looked forward to working closely with him.
"Expect a more exposed Central Bank president. Expect more volatility," said Bruno Scharfstein, a partner at the Rio de Janeiro bank Banco Fonte Cindam.

Franco's designation was also seen as strengthening Malan, nominally Brazil's top economic policy-maker, who of late has been criticized by members of Cardoso's cabinet for not being a more forceful articulator of economic policy.
"Franco's designation clearly had the president's support, and this makes Minister Malan stronger," said Roberto Setubal, president of Banco Itau and head of Febraban, Brazil's Banking Federation.
Franco would become Cardoso's third Central Bank President in two and a half years. Persio Arida, Cardoso's first Central Bank chief, bowed out after six months on the job.
